title: The child dies (2 Samuel 12:15–23)
hook: David fasts while the child lives, then rises and eats: "I shall go to him"

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's answer to Nathan, with no because. Your line was no because, no but. Did you stop before the excuse? Today, the consequence Nathan named arrives, and David does something no one around him expects. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

The servants are whispering in the hallway, and that is how the king finds out. Night after night he has lain on the ground. He hasn't eaten. The elders of his house stood over him and tried to lift him up, and he wouldn't get up and wouldn't eat with them. Now the child is gone, and nobody wants to be the one to say it. If he was like this while the boy lived, they ask each other, what will he do when he hears? David sees them whispering. He asks: is the child dead? And they say: he is dead.
screen: `ON THE GROUND ALL NIGHT.` → `THE SERVANTS WHISPER.` → `IS THE CHILD DEAD?`

segments.voice: This part of the chapter opens with a hard sentence: the Lord struck the child, and he was very sick. Readers have wrestled with that line, and it's fair to let it stay hard. The child did nothing. The text doesn't explain it away, and neither will we. What it does tell, in detail, is what David did. While the boy was alive, David pleaded with God for him, fasted, and lay on the earth. On the seventh day the child died. And then the surprise. David gets up from the ground. He washes, anoints himself, changes his clothes. He goes into the house of the Lord and bows down. Then he comes home, asks for food, and eats. His servants can't make sense of it. You wept while he lived, and now you rise and eat? His answer is plain. While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, because I thought: who knows? Maybe God will be gracious, and the child will live. But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? "I shall go to him," he says, but he will not return to me. Readers hear that last line in more than one way. Some hear only the grave: every person will one day go where the child has gone. Some hear a quiet hope of meeting again. The text doesn't decide for us. What it shows clearly is a turn. As long as something could still change, David fought for it with everything he had. When it could no longer change, he stopped fighting it, washed his face, and went on living. That isn't the same as not caring. The man who rises and eats is the same man who lay on the ground all night.
screen: `THE CHILD IS STRUCK. IT STAYS HARD.` · `FASTING WHILE HE LIVES.` · `HE RISES, WASHES, EATS.` · then, large: `I SHALL GO TO HIM.` · then: `FIGHT WHILE IT CAN CHANGE. THEN RISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one thing that can't be changed. Settle, and breathe. Let something come to mind that you keep pushing against: a loss, a decision that's already made, a door that has closed. Ask honestly, is there anything left I can do? If there is, name it, and save it for later. If there isn't, let your hands open on your lap, palms up. Breathe out slowly. You're not saying it doesn't matter. You're letting it be what it is. If you pray, you can place it before God. The bell holds the time.
Gets up. What David did after days of fasting and grief, before he washed, ate, and went on living. Today's word.

Your line: I shall go to him. Today, if something can't be changed, wash your face and take one ordinary step. And look back at this week: swifter than eagles, holding nothing back, chesed, power can blind, the judge has written his own verdict, no because, no but, and I shall go to him. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: In Jewish mourning, people grieve fully and then, step by step, return to ordinary life; David's rising and eating after the child's death is sometimes taught alongside those customs, though the customs come from later law.

fork.setup: you're one of David's servants. the child has died, and the king hasn't eaten for days. what do you do?
options: hold back and whisper with the others.
bring him food and say nothing.
fork.reveal: they were afraid to tell him and whispered among themselves; David saw it and asked them himself.

original.note: Hebrew: I am going to him, from David's answer in 2 Samuel 12:23.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king who stopped caring.
what it means: David fought for the child while anything could change, then accepted what couldn't, and went on living.
what a scholar hears: I shall go to him is left open: the grave that waits for everyone, or a hope of meeting again.
